title: Error budget policy review (enforcement + exceptions) - Hosted vs Dedicated
topics: Policy goals and where enforcement lives (CI gate vs rollout tooling vs routing controls)
Warn-only vs soft-block vs hard-block modes
Exception/override process (who, TTL, audit trail, scope)
Dedicated nuances (pool isolation, readiness SLI, capacity incidents vs code changes)
Alerting and burn-rate thresholds; multi-window burn alerts
Comms triggers and Support alignment (what we tell customers when budgets burn)
summary: Team reviewed the draft error budget policy with a focus on enforcement mechanisms (CI/release gates, canary progression blocks, routing mitigations) and the exception workflow. Main debate: whether to allow hard blocking immediately when budgets are exhausted, versus starting warn-only / soft-block to avoid blocking urgent fixes and capacity-related actions. Dedicated tier concerns: customers expect more predictability; budget policy must not prevent capacity remediation, and pool readiness should be treated differently than API 5xx/latency. Agreement trending toward phased enforcement: warn-only across most services, soft-block for canary progression in a pilot set, and hard-block reserved for sustained multi-window burn with explicit oncall approval. Overrides should be time-bound, scoped (tier/service/region), and logged with an incident or change ticket reference.
next_steps: Aisha to update the policy doc with a phased enforcement table (warn-only → soft-block → hard-block) and explicit criteria per tier.
Connor to propose an exception/override rubric (approvers, required context, TTL defaults, audit logging fields).
Ethan/Benji to confirm how the control plane budget-check endpoint will support scoped queries (tier/service/region) and return human-readable reasons for CI.
Lauren to validate Dedicated-specific language: what actions remain unblocked during capacity remediation and how readiness SLI impacts gating.
Rafael to align burn-rate thresholds with the org standard multi-window alerts and reduce noise (grouping + anti-flap).
Marissa/Paula to confirm how Console/Rollouts will surface 'blocked due to budget' vs 'warning' UX and override affordance.
action_items: Aisha Bello - Add Dedicated carve-outs: capacity remediation and pool readiness incidents should not be blocked by release gates; clarify what 'change freeze' means for Dedicated - Due 2026-02-09
Connor O'Brien - Draft override process section (who can approve, TTL defaults, required ticket/incident link, auditing) - Due 2026-02-10
Benji Okafor - Ensure budget-check API returns scope + recommended action (warn/soft-block/hard-block) and includes policy version - Due 2026-02-12
Jordan Lee - Confirm policy engine schema supports tier-aware overrides and backward compatibility for existing tenants - Due 2026-02-12
Rafael Mendes - Propose burn alert thresholds (fast burn / slow burn) per tier and list which ones page vs ticket - Due 2026-02-11
Lauren Bishop - Review Dedicated customer expectations and suggest comms language for 'budget at risk' states - Due 2026-02-13
transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Title: Error budget policy review (enforcement + exceptions) - Hosted vs Dedicated
Date: 2026-02-05 4:00 PM PT
Duration: 53 min
Attendees: Sean Gallagher, Rafael Mendes, Aisha Bello, Connor O'Brien, Ethan Park, Benji Okafor, Jordan Lee, Mina Haddad, Ravi Menon, Lauren Bishop, Marissa Cole, Sahana Iyer, Devon Price, Amara Diallo, Logan Wright, Nadia Rahman, Neha Kapoor, Priya Natarajan


[00:00] Sean Gallagher: Cool, thanks everyone. This one is basically the policy review, enforcement and exceptions. The SLO definitions are in flight, but today we need to land the “what happens when you burn” behavior. I’m going to be annoying about specifics.

[00:16] Rafael Mendes: And we should leave with a call on warn-only vs block, at least for the first rollout.

[00:22] Priya Natarajan: Yep. Also want clarity where enforcement lives. Is it CI? Is it rollout tooling? Is it routing? Probably all of the above, but we need a clean mental model.

[00:34] Aisha Bello: I shared the doc in chat, latest draft is yesterday’s. Section 4 is enforcement modes. Section 5 is exceptions.

[00:41] Neha Kapoor: And just to level set, exec intent is not “block shipping forever,” it’s “make error budget real.” So if we pick warn-only forever, we fail.

[00:52] Sean Gallagher: +1. Ok. Let’s do enforcement first. Ethan, can you summarize what’s realistic in the control plane right now?

[01:01] Ethan Park: Sure. We can expose a budget-check endpoint that pipelines call during deploy, or rollout controller calls during canary. The endpoint can answer “budget state for this scope.” Scope being tier, service, and optionally region/model/route. We need to be careful with label explosion.

[01:19] Benji Okafor: From a CI standpoint, easiest is: a step that hits the endpoint, gets back status: OK / WARN / BLOCK. In warn-only, it never fails the pipeline but posts comment. In block, it fails unless override token.

[01:34] Sahana Iyer: CI is straightforward. The harder part is the rollout tool behavior: if the gate blocks progression, we need a good UX and the override path, otherwise people will just bypass with manual deploy.

[01:46] Marissa Cole: Yeah, and in Console we need to show why it’s blocked. Not just “budget exhausted,” but like “fast burn 10x over 5m window” or “remaining budget < 5%.”

[01:57] Sean Gallagher: Great. Mina / Ravi, routing enforcement?

[02:01] Mina Haddad: We can do mitigation triggered by burn signals: prefer fallback model variants, region failover, and for Hosted potentially protective throttling. But for Dedicated we need guardrails so we don’t route someone’s dedicated traffic into shared hosted, obviously.

[02:17] Ravi Menon: And there’s a subtlety: routing changes can improve SLO quickly, but they’re also changes. So if we freeze changes when budget is low, but the mitigation is a change, we need a policy carve-out.

[02:31] Connor O'Brien: This is my main concern. If policy says “change freeze when budget exhausted,” we need exceptions for mitigations and emergency fixes. Otherwise oncall is handcuffed.

[02:42] Neha Kapoor: Agree. The policy has to distinguish “feature work” from “mitigation / rollback.”

[02:48] Aisha Bello: In draft, I have a line: “Budget exhaustion triggers change restrictions, with exemptions for incident mitigation, rollbacks, and security patches.” But it’s vague.

[02:59] Sean Gallagher: Let’s make it non-vague. Like, what is allowed, who decides, and how it’s recorded.

[03:05] Lauren Bishop: Before we go too deep: Dedicated nuance. If we block deploys on Dedicated when the pool is already struggling, we might prevent fixes. Also sometimes the issue is capacity, not code. So the “freeze” shouldn’t block capacity remediation like scaling up pools.

[03:21] Priya Natarajan: That’s a good point. Capacity changes are changes, but they’re the right change.

[03:27] Logan Wright: On the observability side, also: budget burn could be a data issue. Like we miscount 499s or timeouts, then everyone is blocked for no reason. So we need a “false positive” playbook and an override path that doesn’t take 6 hours.

[03:44] Nadia Rahman: +1. Data correctness is not perfect in week one. It will get better, but we shouldn’t create a perverse incentive to disable metrics.

[03:54] Sean Gallagher: So it sounds like phased enforcement is the only sane approach. Question is: what is phase 1. Rafael?

[04:01] Rafael Mendes: Proposal: warn-only in CI for the first 2-3 weeks, while we validate SLIs. But in parallel we do soft-block in canary progression for a pilot set of services where we have confidence—like gateway and routing. Soft-block meaning it requires explicit approval/override, not just “oops it failed.”

[04:22] Devon Price: For rollout tooling, we can implement “pause” rather than “fail.” Like the canary pauses at 10% and says “needs approval” if budget is in a bad state. That’s less disruptive.

[04:36] Sean Gallagher: That’s good. A hard fail in CI is kind of blunt.

[04:40] Neha Kapoor: But we still need a point where it is actually blocking, not just “click approve.”

[04:46] Connor O'Brien: We can define: warn-only for OK->WARN states. Soft-block for BLOCK state, but override requires oncall or SRE manager approval.

[04:55] Jordan Lee: If we do that, we need an auditable override token system. Otherwise it becomes Slack “sure go ahead.” Policy engine can store overrides with TTL.

[05:06] Benji Okafor: We already had a sketch: override token includes scope, reason, TTL, approver. Pipeline passes token to the budget-check endpoint.

[05:17] Amara Diallo: Sorry, quick question: are we sure about the “BLOCK state” definition? Is it literally “budget exhausted,” or is it based on burn rate? Because budget exhausted could be a long-window thing, but burn rate can spike quickly.

[05:30] Aisha Bello: In doc: “At risk” is burn rate thresholds (fast burn). “Exhausted” is remaining budget <= 0 in the 30-day window. But I agree, we probably want block earlier than fully exhausted if we see sustained fast burn.

[05:46] Rafael Mendes: Standard SRE practice is multi-window, multi-burn alerts. Like 2h burn at 14x and 6h burn at 6x, those kinds of things. We can map those to states.

[06:00] Sean Gallagher: Allison isn’t on this call, but we should align with the org burn alert standard doc. For now, can we agree on states: OK / WARN / BLOCK with clear triggers?

[06:11] Priya Natarajan: Yes, but I need the mapping to behaviors.

[06:15] Sean Gallagher: Let’s do the mapping. Aisha, read what you have.

[06:19] Aisha Bello: Okay. Draft behaviors:
- OK: normal.
- WARN (budget at risk): gate posts warning, requires recording a “risk acknowledged” in rollout; allow shipping.
- BLOCK (budget exhausted or severe burn): canary progression blocked; CI fails in hard-block mode; exceptions possible via override.

[06:40] Marissa Cole: “Risk acknowledged” needs to be something real. Like linking a ticket: “we know, we’re taking a calculated risk.” Otherwise it’s checkbox fatigue.

[06:49] Sahana Iyer: In practice we can require a Linear ticket ID in the approval step.

[06:55] Connor O'Brien: Also, “BLOCK” should not block rollbacks. If someone is rolling back, they should be able to do it immediately.

[07:03] Devon Price: We can treat rollback pipelines as always allowed and tag them as “mitigation.” But we need a reliable way to identify them.

[07:12] Ethan Park: The control plane endpoint can accept “change_type” parameter maybe: feature_release | rollback | mitigation | infra_capacity. Then policy says what’s allowed in each state.

[07:27] Jordan Lee: That’s a schema change but feasible. We just have to avoid giving everyone a way to claim “mitigation” for feature release.

[07:35] Priya Natarajan: Right, so who can set change_type? The pipeline? The engineer? That’s a trust boundary.

[07:42] Sean Gallagher: We can start simpler: no change_type parameter yet, but maintain an allowlist: rollback workflows bypass gating, and emergency mitigation has an override requirement.

[07:55] Lauren Bishop: Dedicated question: what about autoscaling changes? Those are often automated. Do we want automated scaling to be blocked because of budget state? That seems backwards.

[08:07] Keiko Yamamoto (speaker label uncertain): Yeah, autoscaling is the fix most of the time.

[08:12] Sean Gallagher: Keiko’s not on invite but okay—good point. Dedicated needs different policy than Hosted.

[08:20] Lauren Bishop: Specifically: Dedicated customers have isolated pools, so a single customer can burn their own budget due to a client bug or sudden traffic. We also have exclusions, but it’s not perfect. If we hard block platform changes because one customer is burning, it’s not fair.

[08:38] Rafael Mendes: That’s why scope matters. Dedicated budgets should be scoped per customer pool, not global. Then gating for gateway/routing might still look at global, but Dedicated should not poison everyone.

[08:50] Nadia Rahman: But per-customer labels are high cardinality. We probably can do it for Dedicated only, since number of dedicated tenants is smaller than hosted traffic.

[09:01] Logan Wright: We can do “customer_pool_id” metrics with controlled retention, and restricted dashboards. But we need to be deliberate.

[09:11] Priya Natarajan: Okay, back to enforcement: do we do hard-block for Dedicated at all?

[09:18] Lauren Bishop: I would say yes eventually, but not until we’ve validated readiness SLI and the capacity signals. Otherwise we’ll block the wrong thing.

[09:28] Sean Gallagher: Dedicated also has pool readiness SLI. Vanessa and Gabe aren’t here, but we need to define how that influences policy.

[09:36] Aisha Bello: Draft says pool readiness is an SLI with its own SLO. If it burns fast, it pages Dedicated oncall. For gating, I didn’t connect it yet.

[09:49] Mina Haddad: For Dedicated, routing mitigations are limited. We can’t fallback to some other shared model. But we can failover within the same dedicated pool region pair maybe.

[10:01] Ravi Menon: Or within a dedicated “burst capacity” pool, if they bought it. But that’s product / contract.

[10:07] Marissa Cole: This is where product and engineering collide. The policy should not assume features that aren’t in the contract.

[10:14] Neha Kapoor: We can keep it operational: mitigation options depend on tier and entitlement. But policy can say “prefer least customer-impacting mitigation.”

[10:24] Sean Gallagher: Let’s ground it. The specific debate: block vs warn-only. I’m hearing: start warn-only broadly, soft-block canary for a pilot, no immediate hard-block in CI. Is anyone opposed?

[10:37] Neha Kapoor: I’m okay with that as long as there’s a date when it stops being toothless.

[10:42] Priya Natarajan: Same. Also I want to ensure soft-block actually changes behavior. Not “click override and proceed.”

[10:50] Connor O'Brien: We can require oncall ack for override in soft-block. Like, it pings #eng-oncall and they approve.

[10:59] Jordan Lee: Or require a named approver list, e.g., SRE manager or director. But that’s heavy.

[11:07] Rafael Mendes: Maybe: for pilot, require SRE oncall approval. For general rollout, require service owner oncall. We can tune.

[11:16] Aisha Bello: Exception handling: what I have is: overrides granted for max 24 hours, must include incident ID or ticket, must be scoped to tier/service/region, and logged.

[11:30] Benji Okafor: TTL default 12 hours might be better. 24 hours is long.

[11:36] Sahana Iyer: Also, overrides should be reusable? Like a token you can pass multiple deploys? Or one-time?

[11:44] Jordan Lee: Reusable within TTL but only for that scope. And include “max uses” maybe, but that’s overengineering.

[11:55] Sean Gallagher: Let’s not overbuild v1. TTL + scope + audit log is minimum.

[12:02] Amara Diallo: Another nuance: what if we’re blocked due to hosted budget, but the deploy is for Dedicated-only service path? Like a dedicated scheduler change. If the gate is global, it will block unrelated stuff.

[12:17] Ethan Park: That’s why the scope should be service-level or tier-level. If the deploy is for dedicated scheduler, it checks Dedicated scheduler budget, not Hosted gateway budget.

[12:29] Priya Natarajan: Which implies we need a service mapping registry. What service maps to which SLO.

[12:35] Aisha Bello: Yes, that’s part of SLO toolkit config. We have a draft mapping of service -> SLI queries.

[12:44] Logan Wright: From metrics side, we need consistent labels: tier, region, route_group, model_family maybe. If we don’t have tier label end-to-end, the budgets are garbage.

[12:58] Nadia Rahman: We’re adding tier propagation gateway -> routing -> runtime. It’s mostly there but there are gaps.

[13:07] Sean Gallagher: Ok. Let’s zoom to Dedicated-specific “what to page vs ticket.” Lauren, what’s your expectation?

[13:14] Lauren Bishop: Dedicated customers expect paging for real service outage or readiness issues. But we shouldn’t page for tiny dips. And we should separate “pool not ready” from “p99 latency.” The “pool readiness” is binary-ish and should page if it’s sustained.

[13:34] Rafael Mendes: So: readiness SLI alert could page oncall; latency burn could ticket unless severe. Hosted is more tolerant; Dedicated is stricter.

[13:45] Neha Kapoor: That’s consistent with tier principles.

[13:48] Marissa Cole: On the product side, we need a clean story: Dedicated has stricter SLOs and different enforcement, but also different mitigations. We don’t want to promise auto-failover if we can’t.

[14:02] Sean Gallagher: Good. Now, exception handling: who can approve.

[14:06] Connor O'Brien: I propose a rubric:
- Standard override: service oncall can approve, TTL 6 hours.
- High-risk override (budget exhausted + hard-block): SRE manager or director approval, TTL 2 hours.
- Blanket overrides should be extremely rare, must link incident, and auto-expire.

[14:29] Priya Natarajan: But if it’s 2 AM, SRE manager isn’t online.

[14:33] Rafael Mendes: Then oncall should be able to approve but with a post-hoc review.

[14:38] Sean Gallagher: That’s reasonable: allow oncall approval but require a post-incident followup and auto-create ticket.

[14:46] Jordan Lee: We can have the override API require an “approver_role”: oncall | sre_manager | exec. But again, trust boundary.

[14:56] Ethan Park: We can integrate with oncall tooling later. V1 can just record the requester and who typed the approval.

[15:05] Sahana Iyer: If approval is “someone typed their name,” that’s weak. But okay for pilot.

[15:11] Neha Kapoor: Pilot is fine, but we need a path to stronger auth.

[15:16] Sean Gallagher: Agreed. We can do SSO-backed approvals later.

[15:20] Aisha Bello: Another open question: what counts as “excluded” from budget. Like customer-side timeouts, invalid auth, misuse. If we exclude too much, budget looks great; if we exclude too little, we block shipping on customer bugs.

[15:38] Nadia Rahman: Specifically 499s. Are they client aborts or our streaming stalling? Our current classification is not perfect.

[15:46] Amara Diallo: We’re adding disconnect taxonomy: client abort vs server-side disconnect. But it’s messy. Some client aborts are because we were slow.

[15:58] Sean Gallagher: That’s why we use multiple indicators: TTFT, stream disconnects, and 5xx. If TTFT is bad and client aborts spike, that’s on us.

[16:11] Logan Wright: For policy, we can define: client aborts are excluded unless correlated with latency SLI breach. But that’s complex.

[16:22] Rafael Mendes: We should not do conditional exclusions in v1. Too hard to explain.

[16:27] Priya Natarajan: Agree. Keep it simple.

[16:30] Sean Gallagher: Okay, so for now: exclude invalid auth, 4xx user errors, explicit client cancels maybe? But streaming disconnects due to server disconnect count as failures.

[16:44] Aisha Bello: That matches the SLI spec. We’ll document.

[16:48] Marissa Cole: Coming back to enforcement: when budget is at risk, what is the comms? Who tells Support? Do we trigger status page automatically?

[17:00] Sean Gallagher: That’s another doc, but policy can say “budget burn is an internal signal; status page triggers are based on customer impact.” Still, we can have triggers: if Hosted availability SLO is projected to breach, we alert Support.

[17:15] Neha Kapoor: I want that. Support shouldn’t learn from Twitter.

[17:20] Lauren Bishop: Dedicated escalations are even more sensitive. If a dedicated pool is burning, CS needs to know early.

[17:28] Rafael Mendes: We can have incident-bot post “budget at risk” summaries to #support-escalations. But we need to avoid spam.

[17:40] Logan Wright: That’s doable with grouping and thresholds.

[17:44] Sean Gallagher: Okay, let’s lock decisions.

[17:48] Sean Gallagher: Decision 1: Phased enforcement.
- Phase A: warn-only CI gates everywhere; soft-block canary progression for pilot services.
- Phase B: expand soft-block; optionally introduce hard-block for certain change types.
Everyone okay?

[18:06] Priya Natarajan: Yes.

[18:07] Neha Kapoor: Yes, with timeline.

[18:10] Sean Gallagher: Decision 2: Override requirements.
- Overrides scoped, time-bound, logged, require ticket/incident link.
- Oncall can approve in pilot; later we harden auth.
Okay?

[18:25] Connor O'Brien: Yep.

[18:27] Jordan Lee: Yes.

[18:28] Sahana Iyer: Yes.

[18:30] Sean Gallagher: Decision 3: Dedicated carve-outs.
- No gating that blocks capacity remediation and readiness incident response.
- Dedicated budgets scoped per pool (where feasible) to avoid cross-customer blast.
Lauren, okay?

[18:48] Lauren Bishop: Yes, with the caveat that per-pool metrics must be restricted.

[18:53] Logan Wright: We can do restricted dashboards.

[18:56] Nadia Rahman: And keep the label cardinality budget under control.

[19:02] Sean Gallagher: Great.

[19:04] (crosstalk)

[19:06] Marissa Cole: One more: “soft-block” definition. Is it “pause canary and require explicit approval,” or “block progression automatically with no override?”

[19:16] Devon Price: I recommend pause + approval. Otherwise folks will just bypass outside tooling.

[19:23] Priya Natarajan: Agree. The goal is to force conversation.

[19:27] Neha Kapoor: But the approval must be meaningful. Maybe require SRE oncall or service owner oncall.

[19:35] Rafael Mendes: For pilot, SRE oncall. For later, service owner oncall + SRE notified.

[19:44] Sean Gallagher: Okay.

[19:46] Ethan Park: Operationally, budget-check endpoint should return “recommended approver.” We can embed that from config.

[19:54] Jordan Lee: That’s nice-to-have.

[19:57] Sean Gallagher: All right. Let’s talk timeline quickly.

[20:01] Rafael Mendes: If we want warn-only in CI next week, we need the endpoint stable and the initial budgets computed. Might be tight but possible for gateway and routing.

[20:12] Benji Okafor: Endpoint is mostly ready. The bigger issue is budget computation job and data model. But for warn-only, we can compute from Prometheus queries on the fly. Not ideal but okay.

[20:26] Logan Wright: On-the-fly queries might be expensive and flaky.

[20:29] Benji Okafor: True. We can cache results for a few minutes.

[20:34] Nadia Rahman: Please be careful. If the query times out, what does CI do? It shouldn’t block.

[20:42] Sean Gallagher: Policy: if budget status is unknown due to system failure, treat as WARN not BLOCK. And open a ticket. Agree?

[20:53] Priya Natarajan: Yes. Don’t stop deploy because the SLO tool is down.

[20:58] Neha Kapoor: But track it. Otherwise we’ll run “unknown” forever.

[21:03] Sean Gallagher: Cool. That’s another explicit policy statement.

[21:07] Aisha Bello: I’ll add “unknown state handling.”

[21:11] Connor O'Brien: Also define: “emergency fix” is allowed with override even when budget exhausted. But should be a rollback-first posture.

[21:21] Marissa Cole: Can we codify “rollback first”? It’s more of a norm.

[21:25] Sean Gallagher: We can write: “During exhaustion, prefer mitigations/rollbacks; feature releases require explicit risk acceptance and SRE approval.”

[21:38] Lauren Bishop: For Dedicated, “feature releases” are often customer-requested changes. Still, we can require extra approval.

[21:46] Priya Natarajan: Great.

[21:48] (pause)

[21:50] Sean Gallagher: Any strong objections left?

[21:53] Amara Diallo: Just a caution: if we tie too much to streaming disconnect, we’ll block often because clients drop. Make sure the SLI spec is right.

[22:03] Aisha Bello: Noted. That’s in the SLI spec doc and we’ll tune.

[22:08] Logan Wright: And please, cardinality. If we try to do per-model per-route per-region per-tenant, we will melt the metrics bill.

[22:17] Nadia Rahman: We can pick a small set of route groups and model families for Hosted. Dedicated can be more granular.

[22:24] Sean Gallagher: Perfect. That’s a separate workstream but it impacts feasibility.

[22:29] Priya Natarajan: Okay, wrap-up.

[22:32] Sean Gallagher: Recap:
1) We do phased enforcement: warn-only CI; soft-block canary for pilot.
2) Overrides: scoped, TTL, require ticket/incident link; audit log.
3) Dedicated: carve-outs for capacity remediation; scope budgets per pool when feasible; treat readiness separately.
4) Unknown budget state: WARN not BLOCK.
Aisha and Connor will update docs; Ethan/Benji/Jordan will align API + schema.

[23:05] Neha Kapoor: And include a timeline for when we move from warn-only to real gating.

[23:10] Rafael Mendes: We’ll propose that after we backtest for a couple weeks.

[23:15] Marissa Cole: I’ll sync with Paula on the Console/Rollouts UX copy. “Blocked due to budget” needs a good explanation.

[23:22] Sean Gallagher: Great. Thanks all.

[23:27] Meeting ended (recording continued briefly)

[23:31] Speaker 3: (unintelligible) should we schedule the next review?

[23:35] Sean Gallagher: Yeah, Talia will.

[23:38] End of transcript.
